newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: SOCCER-COLOMBIA PREPARE FOR LIFE WITHOUT VALDERRAMA.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-COLOMBIA PREPARE FOR LIFE WITHOUT VALDERRAMA.

text.p: Like a Bogota bus which has no ornaments dangling in front of the windscreen, no stickers covering the windows and no salsa blaring from the stereo, there is something strangely missing from Colombia's Copa America team.
The familiar figure with a wild mop of curly hair, who strolls nonchalantly around the field laying off quick, incisive passes to his team mates, is no longer there.
Carlos Valderrama, a permanent fixture in the side for more than a decade, is being rested from the Copa America.
Coach Hernan Dario Gomez promises that the 36-year-old will be back for Colombia's remaining World Cup qualifying matches and for the finals next year if, as looks likely, Colombia qualify.
But the absence of a player who has played in every Copa America since 1987 is the first sign that an era is about to end.

Valderrama, who has never produced his best on the world stage, is often criticised for his apparently poor work rate and seeming lack of interest in what is going on around him but the Colombians say he will be sorely missed.
In the days before Valderrama, Colombian soccer had been famous only for the pirate league it organised after the Second World War.

Nowadays, Colombia, who face Brazil in their final group game on Thursday, are seen as one of the powers of South American soccer and a team that, although not always delivering what they promise, always have to be taken seriously.

"Of course we have suffered from Valderrama's absence. He is a man who has given us an identity and if he is not there, the team is left without guidance," Gomez said. "He will not be possible to substitute."
Gomez has rested other players who have become fixtures for the best part of 10 years such as Freddy Rincon, Leonel Alvarez, Antony de Avila and Faustino Asprilla, a more recent arrival on the scene.
His plan at the Copa America is to find out who is capable of replacing the players who have brought Colombian soccer out of obscurity and at the very least keep it at the level it is today.
"They are all big absences and a big change after so many years. This is a team that is being formed and hasn't played any international matches, therefore we suffer highs and lows," he said.
To prove his point, Colombia's Copa America performance so far consists of a 2-1 defeat to Mexico, when they conceded two early goals but dominated the second half, and a 4-1 win over Costa Rica.

One high is 21-year-old Neider Morrantes from Atletico Nacional, who scored twice on his debut against Costa Rica. The fact that a lack of firepower in attack has been one of Colombia's biggest problems made his performance all the more encouraging.
Another find is Victor Hugo Aristizabal, 24, who plays in Brazil for Sao Paulo and was second top scorer in this year's Sao Paulo championship.
Hamilton Ricard, Asprilla's temporary replacement, scored a crucial equaliser when Colombia drew 1-1 away to Uruguay in their last World Cup qualifier and also scored against Mexico.
The lows have been the number of chances wasted by the team's forwards, Ricard included, and the blunders of goalkeeper Farid Mondragon and Miguel Calero, who replaced Mondragon against Costa Rica.

Most of the stalwarts are likely to return for the next World Cup qualifier away to Chile on July 5. These include Asprilla, who missed the last two World Cup games through suspension after being sent off against Paraguay for fighting with rival goalkeeper Jose Luis Chilavert.
Gomez could not find enough good words to say about Asprilla, who is sometimes portrayed as a problem player.
"Faustino is a very complete player. As far as I am concerned he can play in any country in the world. He is very professional," he said.
"I wouldn't like to comment on the decisions a fellow coach makes. Personally, I would never consider leaving Faustino on the bench.

"I have never had any trouble and I wish that all professional players were like him. He's a shy person and he doesn't say a lot. The problem is he is famous. He is a public figure, therefore he is news and every little thing he does gets pounced on."
